opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that search engines kind of require you to already know the right words. If you know the name of the concept, or the term of art, you can find it pretty quickly. But a lot of the time, the hard part is that I have this vague sense of what I'm looking for, and I don't know what it's called, or whether it even has a name. With a model, I can just describe the thing in my own clumsy language, like, "There's this phenomenon where such and such happens, is there a name for that?" And it'll usually say, "Oh, you're probably thinking of X," and then suddenly I have the vocabulary to go dig deeper.

The other piece is that you can have a back-and-forth. With search, every query is kind of starting over. With a model, I can say, "No, that's not quite it, it's more like this," and it narrows in. That's much closer to asking a knowledgeable friend than querying an index. It's especially useful when I'm getting into a field I don't know much about, where I don't even know what the right questions are yet. The model can sort of help me figure out the shape of the territory before I go read primary sources.

And I'd add that I still verify things that matter. Models can be confidently wrong, so I treat it as a really good starting point rather than the final word. But as a way of getting from "I don't know what I don't know" to "okay, now I know what to look up," it's been genuinely transformative for me.

r001.rationale: The response says search requires knowing the right words and that a vague question can be hard to name, but it does not explain that extensive context makes a search query unwieldy.

r002.rationale: The response describes models interpreting a rough description and refining through back-and-forth, but does not state that they answer by integrating extensive context supplied by the user.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's most useful is exactly that case — where you don't even know the right words. Like with search, you need the keyword. You need to know what the thing is called before you can find it. And a lot of the time the problem is that I have some vague sense of what I want, I can describe the shape of it, but I have no idea what term people use for it.

So a concrete example: I'll be reading some paper and there's some technique, and I'm like, "This feels like it should be related to this other thing I vaguely remember from a different field." And I can just describe both halves to the model, really loosely, and it'll go, "Oh, you're thinking of X, and yeah, there's a connection here." And then I have the term, and from there I can go search, read the actual paper, whatever. The model is sort of the step that gets me from "fuzzy thing in my head" to "thing I can actually look up."

The other case is just asking dumb questions. If I'm trying to understand something outside my area, I don't want to go find an expert and ask them what's probably a very basic question. With the model I can ask the basic question, then the follow-up, then the follow-up to that, and go as deep as I want without feeling like I'm wasting anyone's time. And it'll meet me at whatever level I'm at. I think people underrate how much friction that removes — a lot of things I just wouldn't have bothered learning before because the cost of getting started was too high.

I will say, I do still check things. For anything that matters, I treat it as a starting point rather than the final answer. But as a way to orient — to figure out what question I should even be asking — it's really good.

r001.rationale: The response says search is hard when you do not know the right terms and describes having only a vague sense of what you want. It does not explain that extensive context makes a question unwieldy to express as a search query.

r002.rationale: The response says the speaker can loosely describe two ideas to a model, which helps identify a term and a connection. It does not clearly state that the model answers by integrating extensive user-supplied context.

astra-6.text:
One thing I find really useful is that you can describe what you’re confused about without knowing the right terminology. With a search engine, you often need to know enough about the answer to formulate the query. With a model, you can say, “I have this vague idea. It’s sort of like this, but that’s not quite what I mean.” And it can suggest a few things you might be pointing at.

Even if its first answer isn’t right, you can go back and forth: “No, I mean something more like this.” Sometimes the useful outcome is just learning that there’s a name for the thing you were thinking about. Then you can search for it and check more reliable sources. It helps you get from a fuzzy question to one you can actually investigate.

r001.rationale: The response says search queries can be hard to formulate without knowing the right terminology, but does not explain that extensive context makes a query unwieldy.

r002.rationale: It describes giving a model a vague idea and refining the exchange, but does not state that models answer by integrating extensive user-supplied context.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing I find really useful is being able to ask a question before I know the right vocabulary. With search, you often need to know what the thing you’re looking for is called. With a model, I can say, “I have this vague idea; it’s something like this, but not quite,” and give a few examples. It can suggest concepts or ways of framing the question, and I can say, “No, that’s not what I meant,” and keep going.

Even when the answer isn’t reliable enough to take at face value, that can get me to a point where I know what to search for and what I need to check. It’s useful for turning confusion into a more concrete question.
